content:
When a job candidate is all but guaranteed to get the gig, or a movie seems destined to sweep awards season, you might see it referred to as “a shoe-in.”

That’s not quite right, however. The correct spelling is “shoo-in,” yet the erroneous “shoe-in” still makes many appearances in writing (much like “get down to brass tax” for “get down to brass tacks”). It turns out there’s quite a sketchy history behind the term as well.

Here’s a little history behind “shoo-in.”

“The term ‘shoo-in’ comes from the early 20th century, originating from American horse racing to refer to allowing a horse to win easily, often through a rigged or fixed race,” Madeline Enos, a language trends expert at the learning platform Preply, told HuffPost. “The phrase combines the verb ‘shoo,’ meaning to drive something in a direction ― ‘shooed across the finish line’ ― and the preposition ‘in.’”

Esteban Touma, a cultural and linguistic expert at the language learning platform Babbel, traced its evolution.

“To ‘shoo’ a horse in was to usher it home as the winner, and a ‘shoo-in’ was originally a race that had been fixed so that a particular horse would win,” he explained. “The earliest dictionary citation is from 1928, although the verb was being used in racing circles a little earlier.”

Basically, corrupt jockeys would deliberately hold back their own horses so that a predetermined winner could be “shooed” across the finish line to victory.

“By the 1930s, ‘shoo-in’ was being applied to any horse expected to win comfortably, and by the 1960s it had moved into politics and general use, where it now means a candidate or contender who is all but certain to succeed,” Touma said.

Over time, the term lost its shady undertones.

“Today, the negative connotations have faded, with the term becoming used as a noun, expanding to politics, business and everyday speech to describe the winner themselves,” Enos said. “Now, if someone says ‘he is a shoo-in,’ it simply means the person is guaranteed a win or success, taking on a more positive light.”

Still, a trace of the original remains.

“The suggestion of foul play has largely dropped away, though the sense that the outcome was settled before the contest began is still there,” Touma noted.

As for the word “shoo,” it has its own interesting story (which can even be linked to a beloved pie).

“The ‘shoo’ itself is the same word used to drive off flies, chickens or small children,” Touma said. “It’s an imitative sound, which is why so many languages have something similar ― sciò in Italian, xô in Portuguese, sio in Polish, кыш in Russian, schas in Swedish and husch in German. They nearly all rely on the same hushing, sibilant noise.”

So why do people write “shoe-in”?

“Many people spell it ‘shoe-in’ because the two words sound identical and only one of them is familiar,” Touma said. “Most people now meet ‘shoo’ only when waving something away, whereas ‘shoe’ is an everyday word, so the brain reaches for it.”

He added that the choice of “shoe” also might make intuitive sense to people ― “something that slips on easily, like a well-fitting shoe, or having a foot in the door.”

Enos agreed that the error is understandable.

“Many people mistakenly assume that this idiom, mistaken as ‘shoe-in,’ quite literally means to get a foot in the door ― another common idiom meaning to take the first step towards a goal,” she said.

There’s also a term for this type of mix-up.

“The misspelling of the term ‘shoo-in’ is a common example of an eggcorn ― when an altered word or phrase is created by mishearing or misinterpreting an unfamiliar expression with a similar-sounding alternative,” Enos said. “In this case, the words ‘shoo’ and ‘shoe’ are pronounced identically in everyday speech, explaining the common misinterpretation.”

Other examples include “free reign” instead of “free rein,” and “peak your interest” for “pique your interest.”

The fading connection to American horse racing over time can help explain the confusion around “shoo-in.”

“As the phrase’s usage widened beyond America and horse racing became less prominent in mainstream culture, it’s easy for many people to mistakenly interchange the less common word ‘shoo’ with the more logical substitution of ‘shoe,’” Enos said.

Language naturally shifts over time, often in ways that reflect how people make sense of it. Touma believes the “shoe-in” for “shoo-in” substitution is a good example.

“This is what linguists call folk etymology, where speakers reshape an unfamiliar word into something more recognizable,” he said. “It happens in every language. English ‘cockroach’ is a reworking of the Spanish cucaracha, and German ‘Hängematte,’ literally ‘hanging mat,’ is a reshaping of a word of Caribbean origin that reached German via Spanish and Dutch.”

So in that sense, perhaps “shoe-in” could be considered part of a long tradition.

“‘Shoo-in’ is a good example of a phrase that outlived its context,” Touma said. “Hardly anyone using it today has a fixed horse race in mind, which is partly why the spelling has drifted. It’s also a good reminder that the ‘wrong’ spelling is rarely random. It usually reflects an attempt to make sense of a word, and that is how a lot of the spellings we now consider standard came about in the first place.”
